newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian coffee arrivals 260,000 tonnes by mid-May.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian coffee arrivals 260,000 tonnes by mid-May.

text.p: A wave of 1996/97 coffee arrivals (Oct-Sept) at Ivorian ports slowed to a trickle by May 12 when arrivals totalled 260,000 tonnes -- up from 155,000 tonnes by that date in 1995/96, industry sources said on Thursday.
Around 3,000 tonnes were registered in the week to May 12, compared to a rate of up to 25,000 tonnes per week in March, when exporters were busy grading a larger than expected crop.
"The coffee is leaving as normal. There didn't seem to be any problem. Once it has been graded it can be shipped without quality problems," said one shipping forwarder.
"A lot of the coffee was probably pre-sold but world price rises have not really had much effect on exports," he added, putting total shipments at 108,000 to mid May.
Ivorian exporters expect a slight pick-up in shipments if prices turn upwards.

"Some exporters are expecting prices to go up soon to around $2,200 (per tonne) even though the price dropped from $2,600 to $2,100 last week," said the forwarder. "There might be more activity then but it won't have much effect."

Arrivals had already matched Ivory Coast's official 1996/97 forecast of 230,000 tonnes by mid-April, with some upcountry buyers then predicting a crop of anything up to 300,000 tonnes. Remaining warehouse stocks could be anything up to 100,000 tonnes.
Despite slow grading of mostly robusta coffee at Ivorian ports, regular shipments are now cutting into the stocks, which have built up since early 1997.
Exporters say local processors will probably take 30,000 tonnes of coffee in 1996/97, leaving up to 200,000 tonnes for export unless markets are found for further amounts of poor grade beans.
One said, "If those are the arrivals figures then I would not expect much more than 200,000 tonnes to be exported."
Official May export data are due out in late June.
